days.title: Their Greatest Challenge
days.summary:
Date: 17/7/1940.

Time: 1320 hours.

Weather: medium clouds at 700m.

Wind speed: 3m/s from 17 degrees.

Situation: while France has fallen, Britain has still not surrendered. As a result, we are probing their defences in preparation for a campaign against them.

Mission: patrol the English coast for enemy aircraft.

Execution: fly at 300km/h at an altitude of 7000m. Fly to Le Havre, then continue on to England. Patrol from Eastbourne to Brighton to Selsey and back. Engage and destroy enemy aircraft on sight if you find yourself in a favourable position. Disengage if the enemy has the advantage. Land at Le Havre Octeville.

Your first priority is the protection of your own life

slides.caption:
3./JG 2 Campaign
Mission 1

Britain's refusal to surrender has done little to dampen the staffel's spirits. Almost everyone is eager for the campaign that is undoubtedly soon to begin, and there's little doubt among them that the war will be over soon.

Despite my doubts, I sometimes think that perhaps they're right. After all, we have already defeated Poland, Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium, and France. Perhaps this war will be over by Christmas?

But then I remember the kings and emperors who failed to invade England in the past, and I begin to doubt again.

slides.caption:
3./JG 2 Campaign
Mission 2

The Spitfire is living up to the reputation it gained over Dunkerque, if not exceeding it. The only major problem it seems to have is its light armament of nothing but machine guns. But even if we don't get immediately shot down, we're still in danger - the wide expanse of the channel makes us all the more vulnerable to a leaking fuel tank or water radiator. The Seenotdienst is there to fish us out if we have to ditch, but even then, the RAF have been known to shoot down our rescue planes.

We've gotten reports that a British convoy will be passing near the Isle of Wight tomorrow morning. We're going to escort some Stukas while they attack it, and hopefully not end up in the drink.

slides.caption:
3./JG 2 Campaign
Mission 3

Someone finally found this damn journal in one of the hangars, and thankfully only checked to see whose it was. I must've left it there before a sortie and returned too exhausted to care or remember where I left it. I can't let that happen again, or I might get reported for wehrkraftzersetzung - after all, I'm not exactly the most optimistic person.

Anyway, after more than a month of testing the RAF and defending attacks against convoys and coastal targets, we're finally going to start attacking the RAF's airfields and their RDF stations. The sooner that air superiority can be achieved, the sooner that the invasion can begin and the war can end.

We're also flying the latest model of the Bf 109, the E-4. It has an automatic prop pitch control system, giving us one less thing to worry about during combat. It also has the new MG FF/M cannons, which can fire an improved 20mm round called the minengeschoss. There's also armour for us, and a new canopy design.

However, I cannot allow myself to become overconfident just because of the E-4's improvements. The RAF's fighters are still dangerous, the Channel is as wide as ever, and the fighting is going to be fiercer from now on. If I'm not careful, I might again find myself forgetting where I left this journal.

slides.caption:
3./JG 2 Campaign
Mission 4

Our offensive against Britain starts in earnest today. Instead of another fighter sweep or escorting another raid against a convoy, we're escorting bombers as they attack inland airfields. That's a problem for us, though. We'll have almost no margin for error, and any pilot who gets hit in their fuel tank or radiators will have a hard choice to make; crash land in England and become a POW, or risk a long flight back over the Channel in a plane that's falling apart. Frankly, I think I'd have a better chance of landing in front of Buckingham Palace than getting back to base in that situation.

Under such conditions, it's hard not to be pessimistic.

We had a depressing reminder of the danger the Channel poses yesterday. We went up to escort a Seenotdienst He 115 while they looked for a Do 17 crew that had ditched in the channel, but they found nothing.

Every day, more fatigue and anxiety creeps into the minds of the staffel. We've taken to calling it 'kanalkrankheit'. But despite that, we still have a job to do. For all my pessimism, I know that we have a better chance of winning this battle if we actually fight it. And the sooner we win this fight, the sooner the war will be over.

missions.title: Mission 8: Date: 16/8/1940 · Escort
missions.briefing:
Date: 16/8/1940.

Time: 1715 hours.

Weather: light clouds at 1300m.

Wind speed: 3m/s from 79 degrees.

Situation: our staffel's escort duties for the day are finished. However, to maintain pressure on the RAF, we have been ordered to fly freie jagd sorties.

Mission: fly a fighter sweep over England and engage targets of opportunity.

Execution: fly a sweep over Portsmouth, Brighton, and Eastbourne at 6000m and 300km/h. Only attack enemy aircraft if you are in an advantageous position. After reaching Eastbourne, land at Le Havre Octeville.

Your first priority is the protection of your own life and aircraft. Your second priority is to protect the lives and aircraft of your fellow pilots. Your third priority is the destruction of enemy aircraft.

slides.caption:
3./JG 2 Campaign
Mission 8

Today bought us yet another long flight over the Channel. Fortunately, though, the Stukas' target of Tangmere was on the coast, and we didn't run into any Spitfires. That being said, the Hurricane is hardly a pushover, especially if they catch you at lower altitudes.

But the day isn't over yet. We have yet another flight across the Channel ahead of us, though thankfully we won't be stuck escorting Stukas this time. That being said, I'll still be glad when I get back to base.

slides.caption:
3./JG 2 Campaign
Mission 9

No attacks have been ordered for today, thankfully. I guess that Fat Hermann finally realised that we need to rest if our aircrew and aircraft are going to perform at their best. I doubt anyone will miss flying over the Channel for a day, unless they're that desperate for a Knight's Cross.

Of course, this means that the RAF also has a day to rest and recover. We have to break them soon, before we're forced to rest again.

slides.caption:
3./JG 2 Campaign
Mission 10 

Yesterday was less restful than we'd expected. A formation of Blenheims attacked the invasion barges at Le Havre in the evening, and we, of course, had to scramble and try to force them away. Thankfully, Blenheims aren't very well armed - all they have is one fixed machine gun in the wing and another in a dorsal turret, so all we have to do is attack from below.

There's no resting today, though. We're escorting Stukas to attack an airfield at Thorney Island, and there's no doubt that the RAF will be waiting for us. After all, their fighters were able to rest as well yesterday.
